title: Local Euclidean spaces
body: A manifold is the mathematical setting for a space that may be curved or globally complicated while still looking locally like ordinary coordinate space. In GR the spacetime arena is modelled as a four-dimensional smooth manifold before a metric is added.

title: Definition
body: A smooth manifold is a set that can be covered by coordinate patches whose overlaps are related by smooth \cref{Coordinate transformations}{math.coordinate_transformation}. The definition separates the idea of nearby points and smooth functions from any particular measuring rule for distance or time.

title: Terrain survey: one surface
body: In the module's terrain survey, the complete ground surface is the manifold \(M\). It is the same underlying collection of ground points regardless of which board labels them. Temperature \(T\) and the measured curvature estimate \(K\) attach scalar values to those points, while no single scientist needs coordinates for the entire site.

title: Coordinates as labels
body: A coordinate chart assigns numbers to points in some local region of a manifold. The numbers are labels rather than physical structure: changing the chart changes the component description without changing the underlying point.

title: Definition
body: A coordinate chart on a manifold is a one-to-one map from an open region of the manifold to an open region of \(\mathbb R^n\). An atlas is a collection of compatible charts whose overlaps are related by \cref{Coordinate transformations}{math.coordinate_transformation}.

title: Terrain survey: one board
body: Scientist \(i\) works on a small region \(U_i\) and uses a straight grid on a rigid tangent board to define \(x_i:U_i\rightarrow\mathbb R^2\). Ground points are mapped smoothly and one-to-one onto the board, whose axes may be differently scaled and need not be perpendicular. The board is a coordinate reference: it approximates the local geometry but does not assert that the whole patch is exactly flat.

title: Changing labels, not points
body: A coordinate transformation changes the numerical labels assigned to manifold points while leaving the points themselves unchanged. In GR this freedom is larger than the Lorentz transformations of SR: curved spacetime generally needs arbitrary smooth changes between local coordinate charts.

title: Definition
body: Given two overlapping charts \(x^\mu\) and \(x'^\mu\), a coordinate transformation is the smooth transition rule \(x'^\mu\coloneqq x'^\mu(x)\) on the overlap. The inverse rule \(x^\mu=x^\mu(x')\) lets the same point be described in either coordinate system.

title: Terrain survey: reconciling neighbours
body: A peg in the overlap of two survey patches has board coordinates \(x^a\) for one scientist and \(y^b\) for the other. Their agreed rule \(y^b=y^b(x^1,x^2)\) relates two descriptions of that same peg. It may be nonlinear despite both boards having straight grids, because their tangent planes, projections, scales, orientations, and obliqueness differ.

title: Jacobian of the change
body: The derivatives \(\partial x'^\mu/\partial x^\nu\) form the Jacobian of the coordinate transformation. Later tensor components will use this Jacobian to change their numerical components while preserving the underlying geometric object.

title: Lorentz transformations as a special case
body: The \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations} are special coordinate transformations between inertial frames in flat spacetime. General coordinate transformations need not be linear, global, or tied to inertial observers.

title: Not a change of physics
body: Changing coordinates is not the same as changing the physical situation. A badly chosen coordinate system can make simple geometry look complicated, and a well chosen one can simplify a calculation, but neither changes the manifold point or the coordinate-independent statement being described.

title: A history through spacetime
body: A worldline is the curve traced by a particle, observer, clock, detector, or light signal through spacetime. It turns a sequence of \cref{Spacetime events}{sr.spacetime_event} into one geometric object.

title: Definition
body: A worldline is a parametrized curve \(x^\mu(\lambda)\) in spacetime. The parameter \(\lambda\) labels points along the curve; for a massive clock or particle it is often convenient to use \cref{Proper time}{sr.proper_time} \(\tau\).

title: Curve versus coordinate plot
body: The worldline is the underlying curve, not just its appearance on a particular diagram. A \cref{Minkowski diagram}{sr.minkowski_diagram} or a curved-spacetime coordinate chart can display the same worldline with different coordinate shapes.

title: Terrain survey: the mobile probe
body: The survey's mobile probe follows a parametrized surface route \(\gamma:t\mapsto\gamma(t)\in M\). Its board-coordinate track changes formula when it crosses into another patch, but the route does not jump. Strictly this is a curve on the spatial terrain; after time is included as another coordinate, the probe's complete history is a worldline.

title: Tangent direction
body: At each sufficiently smooth point of a worldline there is a tangent vector. In SR this tangent becomes the \cref{Velocity four-vector}{sr.velocity_four_vector} when the curve is parametrized by proper time; in GR the same idea lives in the local tangent space at the event.

title: Timelike and null cases
body: Massive particles and physical clocks follow timelike worldlines. Light follows null worldlines. Spacelike curves can appear in diagrams, but they do not represent the history of a material object or signal.

title: Possible directions at one point
body: A curved manifold has no single global vector space in which every arrow naturally lives. Instead each point \(p\) has its own tangent space \(T_pM\): the vector space of possible instantaneous directions through that point. Velocities, directional derivatives, infinitesimal displacements, and tangents to \cref{Worldlines}{math.worldline} are all tangent vectors.

title: Definition
body: The tangent space \(T_pM\) at \(p\) is the vector space of tangent vectors based at that one point. It has the same dimension as the manifold near \(p\). Coordinates provide a basis \(\partial/\partial x^\mu|_p\), but the space and its vectors do not depend on which coordinates are chosen.

title: From curves to tangent vectors
body: Take a smooth curve \(\gamma(\lambda)\) through \(p\), with \(\gamma(0)=p\). Its velocity at the crossing, \(v\coloneqq d\gamma/d\lambda|_0\), is a tangent vector in \(T_pM\). Many curves can have the same tangent: only their shared first-order direction and speed at \(p\) matter, not how they bend later.

title: Tangent vectors as directional derivatives
body: A tangent vector can also be understood by what it does to smooth scalar functions. If \(f\) is a scalar field, then \(v[f]\coloneqq d(f\circ\gamma)/d\lambda|_0\) is the rate at which \(f\) changes along a curve with tangent \(v\). Curves and directional derivatives are two coordinate-independent ways to describe the same tangent vector.

title: Walking on a curved surface
body: Imagine standing at a point on a sphere. Every possible instantaneous walking velocity lies in the flat plane tangent to the sphere there, even though longer paths curve over the surface. This embedded picture is only an aid: an abstract manifold still has a tangent space even when it is not pictured inside a larger flat space.

title: Terrain survey: growth and motion
body: The terrain is a two-dimensional manifold, so at every ground point \(p\) its tangent space \(T_pM\) is a two-dimensional vector space. The grass-growth direction \(G_p\) and the probe velocity \(\dot\gamma\) lie in that space. The board is a useful picture of the tangent plane at its own reference point. Elsewhere in the patch, however, the coordinate basis vectors are tangent to the surface coordinate curves at that ground point; they are not literally the same fixed arrows drawn on the board.

title: Velocity is local
body: At an event \(p\) on a particle's worldline, the curve's tangent gives its instantaneous spacetime velocity. A later event \(q\) has a different tangent space \(T_qM\). On a curved manifold the two velocity vectors cannot be directly subtracted until a connection or transport rule explains how to compare vectors at different points.

title: Basis and components
body: In coordinates a tangent vector is written \(v=v^\mu\,\partial/\partial x^\mu|_p\). The components \(v^\mu\) and basis vectors both change under a new chart in compensating ways, leaving the geometric vector \(v\) unchanged. The coordinate basis is therefore a description of the vector, not part of the vector itself.

title: Infinitesimal is not finite
body: A tangent vector describes first-order motion at one point; it is not automatically an arrow joining two separated manifold points. Turning a finite separation into a tangent vector requires extra choices, such as a coordinate construction or a geodesic map, and may not be unique.

title: Linear questions about directions
body: The cotangent space \(T_p^*M\) is the dual partner of the \cref{Tangent space}{math.tangent_space}. A tangent vector represents a possible direction at \(p\); a covector is a linear rule that probes such a direction and returns a number. Coordinate readouts, differentials of scalar fields, gradients in covector form, and momenta are important examples.

title: Definition
body: A covector or one-form \(\omega\in T_p^*M\) is a linear map \(\omega:T_pM\rightarrow\mathbb R\). Thus \(\omega(av+bw)=a\omega(v)+b\omega(w)\). The number \(\omega(v)\), also written \(\omega_\mu v^\mu\), is the natural pairing between a covector and a vector and needs no metric.

title: Covectors as linear readouts
body: Think of a covector as a linear measuring instruction attached at \(p\). It can ask how much a direction points across a family of level surfaces, how quickly a scalar reading changes along that direction, or what one coordinate component of the direction is. Different tangent vectors can give the same reading, and all vectors in the covector's kernel give zero.

title: A scalar field supplies a covector
body: For a smooth scalar field \(f\), its differential \(df|_p\) is the covector defined by \(df|_p(v)\coloneqq v[f]\). It returns the directional rate of change of \(f\) along \(v\). Vectors tangent to the level surface \(f=\text{constant}\) give \(df(v)=0\), so \(df\) encodes the local orientation of those level surfaces without requiring a metric.

title: Terrain survey: measuring a direction
body: The temperature readings define a scalar field \(T\), so \(dT_p\in T_p^*M\) measures temperature change along any surface direction. Applied to grass growth, \(dT_p(G_p)\) is positive toward warmer ground, negative toward colder ground, and zero along an isotherm to first order. For the moving probe, \(dT_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=(\partial T/\partial x^i)(dx^i/dt)\), the temperature-change rate caused by its motion through a time-independent field.

title: A directional-change calculation
body: Let \(f(x,y)=x^2+3y\). At \(p=(2,1)\), \(df=4\,dx+3\,dy\). For a tangent vector with components \(v=(1,-2)\), the change along that direction is \(df(v)=4(1)+3(-2)=-2\). The covector turns the direction into one scalar rate.

title: Contours and zero change
body: On a contour map, a tangent direction along a contour produces no first-order change in height, so the height differential evaluates to zero on it. A direction crossing several contours produces a nonzero reading. Calling the differential a perpendicular arrow uses a metric to convert it to a vector; the covector itself is the rule assigning these rates.

title: Dual basis
body: If \(\partial/\partial x^\mu\) is the coordinate basis for tangent vectors, the dual covector basis \(dx^\mu\) is defined by \(dx^\mu(\partial/\partial x^\nu)\coloneqq\delta^\mu{}_{\nu}\). Consequently \(dx^\mu(v)=v^\mu\): each basis covector reads one component of a tangent vector. A general covector is \(\omega=\omega_\mu dx^\mu\).

title: Why covectors appear in physics
body: A wave phase \(\phi\) has covector \(d\phi\), which measures phase change along any spacetime direction. In mechanics a momentum one-form pairs with an infinitesimal displacement or velocity to make a scalar contribution to work or action. These pairings explain why lower-index objects arise naturally rather than merely as vectors with altered notation.

title: Do not assume the metric too soon
body: Tangent vectors and covectors are distinct before a metric is chosen. A nondegenerate metric supplies an additional map between them, written as lowering or raising an index. Familiar Euclidean pictures quietly use this map when they draw a gradient covector as an ordinary perpendicular arrow; the cotangent space itself does not depend on it.

title: Tensors varying over spacetime
body: A tensor field assigns a tensor to each point of a manifold. GR uses tensor fields because equations must be meaningful under arbitrary smooth coordinate changes rather than only Lorentz transformations between inertial frames.

title: Definition
body: A tensor field is a smoothly varying assignment of multilinear maps or tensor products of \cref{Tangent spaces}{math.tangent_space} and \cref{Cotangent spaces}{math.cotangent_space} to points of a manifold. Scalar fields and vector fields are low-rank examples.

title: Point-by-point objects
body: The word field means that the object is assigned point by point. In GR the metric, stress-energy, and curvature are not single global arrays; they are geometric objects that can vary from event to event.

title: Scalars, vectors, and higher tensors
body: A scalar field assigns one number to each point. A vector field assigns a tangent vector. Higher-rank tensor fields have several vector or covector slots and can represent objects such as the spacetime metric or stress-energy tensor.

title: Not just an array of components
body: A tensor field has components in a chosen chart, but it is not merely that component array. Under a \cref{Coordinate transformation}{math.coordinate_transformation}, the components change in a controlled way while the underlying geometric object remains the same.

title: Indices as bookkeeping
body: Index notation compresses tensor statements, but an index can play two roles. It can record the abstract type of tensor slot, or it can label a numerical component after a coordinate basis has been chosen.

title: Definition
body: Abstract index notation writes objects such as \(T^a{}_b\) to show tensor type and contractions without choosing coordinates. Component index notation writes objects such as \(T^\mu{}_\nu\) for the components of that tensor in a selected coordinate system or frame.

title: Component indices
body: This atlas usually uses Greek indices such as \(\mu,\nu,\alpha,\beta\) for spacetime components. Unless otherwise stated, these indices range over the spacetime coordinates of the chart being used.

title: Repeated and free indices
body: A repeated upper/lower index pair is summed over. A free index must appear consistently on both sides of an equation. A repeated index is a dummy label: it can be renamed without changing the meaning of the expression.

title: Indexed need not mean coordinate-bound
body: An equation can be coordinate-independent even when it is written using indices. The test is not whether indices appear, but whether the objects and contractions have the right tensor transformation behaviour.

title: Components that transform correctly
body: The tensor transformation law is the rule that tells how component arrays change when coordinates change. It is what lets a tensor equation keep the same geometric meaning in different charts.

title: Definition
body: A tensor transformation law gives one Jacobian factor for each index when moving between coordinates. Contravariant indices transform with derivatives of the new coordinates with respect to the old; covariant indices transform with derivatives of the old coordinates with respect to the new.

title: One factor per index
body: A higher-rank tensor receives one transformation factor for each index. The index positions are not decoration: they record which Jacobian or inverse-Jacobian factors are needed.

title: Not unchanged components
body: Tensorial does not mean the components stay numerically unchanged. It means the components change by the proper rule so that contractions and equations describe the same geometric statement.
